identity.title: Powered Industrial Truck Pre-Shift Inspection Log

scan.summary: This is a daily pre-shift inspection log for a Toyota propane forklift (model 8FGU25, unit FL-2) at the Portland warehouse, covering September 2026. The log records whether each of 14 safety-critical items passed inspection (✓) or failed (X) before each shift. It is the company's record of compliance with 29 CFR 1910.178(q)(7), which requires powered industrial trucks to be examined before each shift and not used if defects affect safety.
scan.freshness_note: The log runs through 17 September 2026; today is 25 September 2026. The log is current as of its last entry eight days ago. It should have daily entries continuing through today. Check whether inspections are continuing.

conditions.title: Daily inspection before truck placed in service
conditions.evidence_expected: Log entry for each shift showing pass/fail on all inspection items; for this truck, that is: tires, forks, mast, horn, lights, belt, brakes, steering, LPG, extinguisher, data plate, overhead guard, and operator name/initials

conditions.title: Do not place truck in service if defects found
conditions.evidence_expected: Log entries with X marks (defects); on this log, 9 September shows 'X' for Horn and note 'Horn not working'; evidence that truck was taken out of service or defect was corrected before use

conditions.title: Defects must be reported and corrected immediately
conditions.evidence_expected: Maintenance records, work orders, or corrective action documentation; for the horn defect on 9 September, evidence that repair was completed

expected_missing.title: Operator training and certification record
expected_missing.why: OSHA 1910.178(l) requires all operators to be trained, evaluated, and certified as competent; record must show operator name, initial training date, most recent evaluation date, and re-evaluation due date
expected_missing.basis: Similar companies hold operator certification records tied to inspection logs; this log records initials only (M.C., J.R.) and does not track certification status or re-evaluation dates

expected_missing.title: Maintenance work order or repair completion record for defects
expected_missing.why: When 'X' marks appear (horn not working, 9 Sept), employer must document corrective action; no attached record shows horn was repaired or when
expected_missing.basis: OSHA 1910.178(q)(7) requires defects be 'immediately reported and corrected'; best practice companies maintain linked repair records

expected_missing.title: Backup inspection log or second shift log
expected_missing.why: If truck is used after day shift, it must be inspected before each shift per 1910.178(q)(7); this log covers day shift only
expected_missing.basis: Chemical distribution and warehouse operations often run multiple shifts; Portland site hours of operation not confirmed

expected_missing.title: Hour meter reconciliation or service interval tracking
expected_missing.why: Manufacturer maintenance schedules are tied to running hours; log records hours but does not track maintenance due dates or link to service history
expected_missing.basis: Systematic fleet management typically tracks service intervals against hour meter readings to prevent deferred maintenance

scan.confidence_notes: High confidence in what the log shows: it is a clear daily record with dates, shift, hours, checklist items, operator initials, and two notes (horn defect and tank change). The log format and content align with OSHA 1910.178(q)(7) requirements. Confidence is lower on three points: (1) The log ends 9 September 2026; today is 25 September 2026; there is no visibility into whether daily inspections continued through today—the record is not current. (2) The horn defect on 9 September is marked but there is no attached documentation showing corrective action or when the truck returned to service; the log does not prove the truck was taken out of service or the defect was fixed. (3) The log shows only day shift inspections; if the truck operates on other shifts or 24/7, additional shift logs should exist and are not provided. No operator certification records are attached, and OSHA would expect to see those; initials alone do not satisfy 1910.178(l) training documentation. The company has a clear, usable log format and operators are signing off daily, which is good. The gaps are in follow-up documentation and coverage across all shifts.
